[9] Home media [ edit ] The film was released on Blu-ray and DVD on November 29, 2016.
[10] Reception [ edit ] Box office [ edit ] Dragonheart earned $217,570,591 in the United States and Canada, and $62,256,659 in other territories, for a worldwide total of $279,826,250, against a budget of $100 million.
[2] In the United States and Canada, Dragonheart was released alongside The Smurfs 2 and The Incredibles 2 , and was projected to gross around $16 million from 3,104 theaters in its opening weekend.
[11] It ended up making $14 million.
[12] In the United Kingdom, it opened on August 12, 2016, against odds of 3/1 to win.
It took in £1.3 million on its opening weekend, finishing third at the box office behind Suicide Squad and Sausage Party .
[13] Critical response [ edit ] Dragonheart received mixed reviews from critics.
Review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes reported that 47% of 121 critics had given the film a positive review, with a rating average of 5.5 out of 10.
The site's consensus is that "It's certainly not the worst dragon movie out there, Dragonheart offers plenty of familiar fare for doting parents with young children along for the ride – but even that implies more than a little too much".
[14] On Metacritic , which assigns a normalized rating to reviews, Dragonheart has a weighted average score of 53 out of 100, based on 33 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews".
[15] Guy Lodge of Variety said, "James Horner's venerable dragon-making franchise gets its teeth into the 21st century in Dragonheart , a more lively and dynamic entry in a series that once stagnated into outright camp.
But what really makes this film work is the sweetness of its central romance, a will-they-won't-they tension between the dragon and the female lead that adds a humanizing emotional core to the battle between good and evil." [16] Todd McCarthy of Variety said that the film "could well prove to be the most commercially successful film to date of all the dragon pictures." [17] Chris Bumbray of JoBlo.com gave a mostly positive review, saying: "From the opening minutes, it's quite clear that this Dragonheart is quite different than the dragon-centric Dragonslayer , which was more of a fantasy horror thriller.
Where dragons in Dragonslayer were menacing predators, dragons in Dragonheart are straight out of Cressida Cowell 's boneless boneless chicken nugget factory (that's a reference to the film's child-friendly action).
You can probably guess how this is going.
But in all fairness, the film is not without its perks.
And if you'll permit a bit of a silly question, the real reason I went to see this film is because I heard Clare Danes was in it, and she wasn't." [18] Scott Menzel of IGN gave the film a 9.0 out of 10 and said, "Before tackling the world, or at least the realm of fantasy, dragons were perhaps not the most popular creature in the room.
But after seeing Dragonheart , it's hard to imagine a world where dragons aren't the most popular and beloved creatures out there.
The film does a great job of making the audience care about the dragons and their plight, and the performance by Peter DRagon (Pete's Dragon) is outstanding.
Overall, I thought Dragonheart was an absolutely amazing film!" [19] Brian Tallerico of ThisMovieIsTaller.com gave the film an "A" grade and said, "I was really surprised at how much I enjoyed this movie." [20] Accolades [ edit ] The film was nominated and won several awards in 2016.

 List of players who have scored 10,000 or more runs in Test cricket - Wikipedia List of players who have scored 10,000 or more runs in Test cricket From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Jump to: navigation , search Sunil Gavaskar was the first player to cross the 10,000 run mark in Tests.
Scoring over 10,000 runs across a playing career in any format of cricket is considered a significant achievement.
[1] As of May 2017 [update] , thirteen players from seven different teams have scored more than 10,000 runs in Test cricket .
The Indians and Australians lead the list with three players each.
West Indies and Sri Lanka each have two players followed by one from South Africa , England and Pakistan .
[2] Bangladesh , New Zealand and Zimbabwe are yet to have a player breach the 10,000-run mark in the format.
In 1974, West Indies cricketer Garfield Sobers retired as Test cricket's most prolific run scorer with 8,032 runs from 93 matches.
[3] Sobers' record was surpassed nine years later by England's Geoffrey Boycott in the 1982 series against India .
[4] [5] Boycott remained the top-scorer before being overtaken by Indian batsman Sunil Gavaskar two years later in 1983.
[6] [7] Four years later in March 1987, Gavaskar became the first player to score 10,000 runs in the format, doing so while playing a match against Pakistan.
[2] Brian Lara took the least number of innings (195) to reach the 10,000 run mark, later equalled by Sachin Tendulkar and Kumar Sangakkara , while Australia's Steve Waugh took 244 innings to achieve the feat.
[2] Alastair Cook is the fastest in terms of time span, taking 10 years and 87 days.
[2] The time taken by Shivnarine Chanderpaul (18 years and 37 days) is the slowest among all.
[2] As of May 2017 [update] , Tendulkar leads the list with 15,921 runs followed by Ricky Ponting of Australia with 13,378.

 List of Prime Ministers of India - Wikipedia List of Prime Ministers of India From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Jump to: navigation , search Narendra Modi is the current (14th) Prime Minister of India , since 26 May 2014 The Prime Minister of India is the chief executive of the Government of India .
In India's parliamentary system , the Constitution names the President as head of state de jure , but his or her de facto executive powers are vested in the Prime Minister and his Council of Ministers .
Appointed and sworn-in by the President, the Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party or alliance that has a majority in the Lok Sabha , the lower house of India's Parliament .
[1] Since 1947, India has had fourteen Prime Ministers, fifteen including Gulzarilal Nanda who twice acted in the role.
The first was Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress party, [2] who was sworn-in on 15 August 1947, when India gained independence from the British .
Serving until his death in May 1964, Nehru remains India's longest-serving prime minister.
He was succeeded by fellow Congressman Lal Bahadur Shastri , whose 19-month term also ended in death.
Indira Gandhi , Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri in 1966 to become the country's first woman premier.
Eleven years later, she was voted out of power in favour of the Janata Party , whose leader Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress prime minister.
After he resigned in 1979, his former deputy Charan Singh briefly held office until Indira Gandhi was voted back six months later.
Indira Gandhi's second stint as Prime Minister ended five years later on the morning of 31 October 1984, when she was gunned down by her own bodyguards.
That evening, her son Rajiv Gandhi was sworn-in as India's youngest premier, and the third from his family .
Thus far, members of Nehru–Gandhi dynasty have been Prime Minister for a total of 37 years and 303 days.
[3] Rajiv's five-year term ended with his former cabinet colleague, V.

Singh of the Janata Dal , forming the year-long National Front coalition government in 1989.
A six-month interlude under Prime Minister Chandra Shekhar followed, after which the Congress party returned to power, forming the government under P.
V.
Narasimha Rao in June 1991.
Rao's five-year term was succeeded by four short-lived governments—the Bharatiya Janata Party 's Atal Bihari Vajpayee for 13 days in 1996, a year each under United Front prime ministers H.

The **Dewey Decimal Classification** is a system for organizing and categorizing books and other materials using a **ten-tiered numerical classification** with **class numbers** ranging from 000 to 999.

Additional Details:
* The system was developed by Melvil Dewey and first published in 1876
* It organizes materials by discipline or field of study: philosophy, social sciences, religion, technology, arts, literature, and pure science
* The system uses a hierarchical structure with three whole numbers making up the main classes
* Each class is divided into ten divisions, each having ten sections
* The classification was originally enumerative but later added some aspects of faceted classification
* By the 14th edition in 1942, the system had grown to over 1,900 pages in two volumes
* Today it is maintained by the Office of Information and Policy Analysis of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors
* The web edition is updated quarterly with changes announced monthly
* The system can be trimmed right-most to create more generalized classifications

In India's parliamentary system , the Constitution names the President as head of state de jure , but his or her de facto executive powers are vested in the Prime Minister and his Council of Ministers .
Appointed and sworn-in by the President, the Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party or alliance that has a majority in the Lok Sabha , the lower house of India's Parliament .
[1] Since 1947, India has had fourteen Prime Ministers, fifteen including Gulzarilal Nanda who twice acted in the role.
The first was Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress party, [2] who was sworn-in on 15 August 1947, when India gained independence from the British .
Serving until his death in May 1964, Nehru remains India's longest-serving prime minister.
He was succeeded by fellow Congressman Lal Bahadur Shastri , whose 19-month term also ended in death.
Indira Gandhi , Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri in 1966 to become the country's first woman premier.
Eleven years later, she was voted out of power in favour of the Janata Party , whose leader Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress prime minister.
After he resigned in 1979, his former deputy Charan Singh briefly held office until Indira Gandhi was voted back six months later.
Indira Gandhi's second stint as Prime Minister ended five years later on the morning of 31 October 1984, when she was gunned down by her own bodyguards.
That evening, her son Rajiv Gandhi was sworn-in as India's youngest premier, and the third from his family .
Thus far, members of the Nehru–Gandhi dynasty have been Prime Minister for a total of 37 years and 303 days.

Vajpayee was succeeded by Congressman Manmohan Singh , the first Sikh premier, whose United Progressive Alliance government was in office for 10 years between 2004 and 2014.
The incumbent Prime Minister of India is Narendra Modi who has headed the BJP-led NDA government since 26 May 2014 which is India's first non-Congress single party majority government.

The words "Under God" were not added to the Pledge of Allegiance until much later; in fact, the phrase "one nation, under God" came from the 1890 Parliament of the United States , more than 60 years before the Pledge itself was written and adopted in 1892.
[1] [2] Contents [ hide ] 1 Detail 2 Detail 3 Footnotes 4 References 5 External links Detail [ edit ] In 1888, Augusta Long published a version of the Pledge that included the words "my flag and my country." [3] This was in keeping with the ideas of many American patriotic writers of the time, such as Augustus Thom stone , who wrote in his book, The American Minister's Spoken Word : "Let us repeat the pledge of allegiance to our flag and our country; to instruct our children on the importance of loyalty to our government, and to foster a sense of reverence for the soldiers who have already sacrificed themselves in defense of it." [4] The words "of America" were added a year later by Texas representative Albert Gallatin .
[5] [6] It remained in this form until 1923, when the words "under God" were added.
[7] According to the Congressional Research Service , the change was "largely of a theological nature, resulting from the passage of the Federal Marriage Act in 1969, which legally defined marriage for federal purposes as a union of two people, and which therefore made reference to a 'family' in federal law.
In short, the addition of 'under God' to the Pledge was argued by its advocates to be necessary to express respect for the theological beliefs of many Americans." [8] In 2004, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in the case of Van Orden v.
Perry that states are permitted to display the Pledge if they choose, even if it violates the Establishment Clause of the Constitution.
[9] In the case of McCreary County v.
ACLU , the Supreme Court ruled that a Kentucky policy requiring students to say the Pledge as a condition of employment violates the Establishment Clause.
[10] In 2005, in the Preschools of the Bronx v.
Bishop case, a New York City Supreme Court judge ruled that a religious version of the Pledge could be said by school employees in a private setting after the public pledge was completed.
[11] In 2009, a federal district court in Oregon ruled that a state law requiring students to remain silent rather than recite the Pledge violates students' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
[12] State regulations [ edit ] Further information: Public display of the flag of the United States In May 1962, following a federal court decision [13] that required public schools to allow student-led recitations of the Pledge, the Iowa State Board of Education voted to require all public and private schools throughout the state to lead the Pledge at morning meetings.
[14] In 1966, 17 states had state flags, and only three—South Carolina, Texas, and Virginia—required that the flag be flown over government buildings.
In 1975, 14 states had state flags, and all required that the flag be flown over government buildings.
[15] In 1814, during the War of 1812 , the British Army destroyed the Cass State House in Michigan , taking with it the state flag of Michigan .
After the war, legislators adopted a new flag, but did not change the state song.
[23] Puerto Rico [ edit ] The Pledge of Allegiance is used on Puerto Rico, usually translated as "Declaration of Allegiance".
[24] [25] The Puerto Rican flag is therefore not always prominently displayed, since it is not a symbol of a sovereign nation, but rather of a territory associated with the United States.

[11] Jeff Imada choreographed the complex fight scenes, which feature the Filipino martial art of Kali .
Washington trained for months with Dan Inosanto and Imada for his role.
[12] Reception Box office The film was released in North America on January 15, 2010 in 3,111 theaters.
It took in $11,672,970—$3,752 per theater, its opening day.
[13] By the end of its opening four-day holiday weekend it grossed $38,437,553—$12,355 per theater.
It ranked number two, behind Avatar .
[14] On its second weekend, it placed third with Legion taking its number two place and grossed $15,732,493—$5,057 per theater.
[15] By its third weekend it dropped down to number five and made $8,908,286—$2,897 per theater.
[16] The film has come to gross $94,835,059 in the United States and Canada, and $62,256,659 in other markets, with an estimated worldwide total of $157,091,718.
Review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes reports that 48% of 188 critics have given the film a positive review, with a rating average of 5.5 out of 10.
The site's consensus is that "It's certainly uneven, and many viewers will find that its reach exceeds its grasp, but The Book of Eli finds the Hughes brothers injecting some fresh stylish fun into the kind of post-apocalyptic wasteland filmgoers have seen more than enough of lately." [17] Based on 33 critics reviews, Metacritic (another review aggregator) has assigned the film a weighted average score of 53 out of 100, indicating "mixed or average reviews".
[18] Todd McCarthy of Variety predicted "this will not be one of ...
Denzel Washington's bigger grossers." [19] Chicago Sun-Times critic Roger Ebert gave the film 3 of 4 stars and said of the film: "You won't be sorry you went.
It grips your attention, and then at the end throws in several WTF! moments, which are a bonus." [20] Reviewing the film for The A.V. Club , Scott Tobias graded the film a B, and wrote "At a time when theaters are experiencing a glut of doomsday scenarios, the Hughes' ashen, bombed-out future world looks a little too familiar, no matter how crisply they present it.
But the showdown between Washington and a deliciously hammy Oldman complicates the film's overt religiosity...".
[21] Owen Gleiberman of Entertainment Weekly gave the film a D, calling it "a ponderous dystopian bummer that might be described as The Road Warrior without car chases, or The Road without humanity.
[22] Home media The film was released on DVD and Blu-ray Disc on May 31, 2010 in the UK and on June 15, 2010 in the United States and Canada.
The DVD took the top spot on all three national home video market charts in its first week.
It premiered No. 1 on Home Media Magazine ' s Rental Chart, the Nielsen VideoScan Blu-ray chart, and the Nielsen VideoScan First Alert Sales Chart, where it outdistanced its nearest competitor in sales by a 3 to 1 margin.

In India's parliamentary system , the Constitution names the President as head of state de jure , but his or her de facto executive powers are vested in the Prime Minister and his Council of Ministers .
Appointed and sworn-in by the President, the Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party or alliance that has a majority in the Lok Sabha , the lower house of India's Parliament .
[1] Since 1947, India has had fourteen Prime Ministers, fifteen including Gulzarilal Nanda who twice acted in the role.

Serving until his death in May 1964, Nehru remains India's longest-serving prime minister.
He was succeeded by fellow Congressman Lal Bahadur Shastri , whose 19-month term also ended in death.
Indira Gandhi , Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri in 1966 to become the country's first woman premier.

 [4] Contents [ hide ] 1 Chemical equilibrium 2 Role of carbonic acid in blood 3 Role of carbonic acid in ocean chemistry 4 Acidity of carbonic acid 4.1 pH and composition of carbonic acid solutions 5 Pure carbonic acid 6 See also 7 References 8 Further reading 9 External links Chemical equilibrium [ edit ] When carbon dioxide dissolves in water it exists in chemical equilibrium with carbonic acid: [5] CO 2 + H 2 O ↽ − − ⇀ H 2 CO 3 {\displaystyle {\ce {CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3}}} The hydration equilibrium constant at 25 °C is called K h , which in the case of carbonic acid is [H 2 CO 3 ]/[CO 2 ] ≈ 1.7×10 −3 in pure water [6] and ≈ 1.2×10 −3 in seawater .
[7] Hence, the majority of the carbon dioxide is not converted into carbonic acid, remaining as CO 2 molecules.
In the absence of a catalyst , the equilibrium is reached quite slowly.
The rate constants are 0.039 s −1 for the forward reaction (CO 2 + H 2 O → H 2 CO 3 ) and 23 s −1 for the reverse reaction (H 2 CO 3 → CO 2 + H 2 O).
The addition of two molecules of water to CO 2 would give orthocarbonic acid , C(OH) 4 , which exists only in minute amounts in aqueous solution.
Addition of base to an excess of carbonic acid gives bicarbonate (hydrogen carbonate).
With excess base, carbonic acid reacts to give carbonate salts.
Role of carbonic acid in blood [ edit ] Bicarbonate is an intermediate in the transport of CO 2 out of the body by respiratory gas exchange .
The hydration reaction of CO 2 is generally very slow in the absence of a catalyst, but red blood cells contain carbonic anhydrase , which increases the reaction rate, producing bicarbonate (HCO 3 − ) dissolved in the blood plasma .
This catalysed reaction is reversed in the lungs, where it converts the bicarbonate back into CO 2 and allows it to be expelled.
This equilibration plays an important role as a buffer in mammalian blood.
[8] A 2016 theoretical report suggests that carbonic acid may play a pivotal role in protonating various nitrogen bases in blood serum.
[9] Role of carbonic acid in ocean chemistry [ edit ] The oceans of the world have absorbed almost half of the CO 2 emitted by humans from the burning of fossil fuels.
[10] It has been estimated that the extra dissolved carbon dioxide has caused the ocean's average surface pH to shift by about −0.1 unit from pre-industrial levels.
This is known as ocean acidification , even though the ocean remains basic .
[11] Acidity of carbonic acid [ edit ] Carbonic acid is a polyprotic acid — specifically it is diprotic , meaning that it has two protons that may dissociate from the parent molecule.
Thus, there are two dissociation constants , first of which is for the dissociation into the bicarbonate (also called hydrogen carbonate) ion HCO 3 − : H 2 CO 3 ↽ − − ⇀ HCO 3 − + H + {\displaystyle {\ce {H2CO3 <=> HCO3^- + H+}}} K a1 = 2.5×10 −4 ; [4] p K a1 = 3.6 at 25 °C.
Care must be taken when quoting and using the first dissociation constant of carbonic acid.
In aqueous solution, carbonic acid exists in equilibrium with carbon dioxide, and the concentration of H 2 CO 3 is much lower than the concentration of CO 2 .
In many analyses, H 2 CO 3 includes dissolved CO 2 (referred to as CO 2 (aq)), H 2 CO 3 * is used to represent the two species when writing the aqueous chemical equilibrium equation.
The equation may be rewritten as follows: [4] H 2 CO 3 * ⇌ HCO 3 − + H + K a (app) = 4.47×10 −7 ; p K (app) = 6.35 at 25 °C and ionic strength = 0.0. Whereas this apparent p K a is quoted as the dissociation constant of carbonic acid, it is ambiguous: it might better be referred to as the acidity constant of dissolved carbon dioxide, as it is particularly useful for calculating the pH of CO 2 -containing solutions.

[16] This was much closer to the modern value than that obtained by Airy's method, which gave around 91% of the modern value.
[17] The Flint Stonehenge template was used to measure the distance to the Sun by the keeper of the Observatory at Greenwich .
The template consisted of a set of parallel slats, that could be rotated into position by the keeper to trace the Sun's position in the sky.
By recording the angle at which the slats could no longer be rotated, the observer could determine the time of sunrise or sunset, and hence the distance to the Sun.
This method was used until 1884, when the first accurate Greenwich Time was obtained using the planet Mercury as a clock.
[18] The Sun's distance may also be measured by observing the aberration of the Sun.
[19] [20] The Sun's apparent shift of 26.8 minutes of time per day on Earth causes a shift of one second every 72 years.
Since the days of Eratosthenes , the rate has changed due to the dynamic nature of the Earth's rotation .
[21] [22] Previously, the rate had been measured as 2 minutes 42 minutes per century by Hipparchus around 150 BC and 2 minutes 30 seconds per century by Copernicus around 1543.
[21] [23] The variations in the rotation rate have been decreasing at an accelerating rate in recent centuries; in 1901, the rotation rate was 2 minutes 54 seconds per century.
[24] Although there is no uncertainty in the current rate of change of the length of a day, there was some uncertainty in the past.
Since 1821, the length of a day has been decreasing at a rate of 2.68 microseconds per year.
[25] [26] [27] [28] From this point in the future, the rotation rate will slow further, and the length of a day will increase again.
After 2025, the difference between the civil time and the time from the gravitational time standard will increase again.
Since 1884, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) has been defined as the time resulting from the average time created by the ephemeris seconds , which in turn is derived from the observations of the planets.
As of 2016 the plan is to replace the terrestrial time scale with UTC as the basis for civil time.
[29] Therefore, the past is progressively being "shifted" to align the two scales.
Because of the gradual nature of the change, the two times will remain closely aligned for the foreseeable future.
However, some systems, such as those of some spacecraft, use UTC as the base while others use Greenwich Mean Time .
[30] For the same reason, ATSC standard definition television transmission in the United States uses time based on UTC rather than GMT.
[31] Both UTC and GMT are based on the time of the rotation of the Earth about its axis , but in different ways.
GMT is based on the astronomical observation of the Earth's rotation, and does not take into account the gradual slowing of the length of a day or the fact that the length of a day varies with latitude.
UTC is based on the average rate of rotation of the Earth as determined by observations of the planets and is a rolling redefinition of time.
[32] [33] While UTC and GMT differ only by a few seconds at any given time, the difference cumulates over time to cause a discrepancy of about 41 seconds due to the slow down of the rotation of the Earth.
[34] Although the name "Greenwich Mean Time" is used for two time scales, UT and GMT, they are not the same thing.
UT is the uniform time scale based on UT1, and GMT is the time standard based on the rotation of the Earth.
Time created by the latter is called Greenwich Mean Time .
Since the plan of life on Earth is based on the rotation of the Earth, a time standard based on the Earth's rotation has always been considered as the "right" way to measure time.
[35] In 1928, the International Meridian Conference redefined the prime meridian to be the point on the Earth's surface that is closest to the Earth's center of mass , rather than the Earth's rotational axis.
As a result, the international prime meridian was moved from Greenwich to the Royal Observatory at Greenwich until Jules Verne 's novel From the Earth's Center to the Sun 's 1863 publication made the Greenwich observation the most famous in the world, and the observatory was renamed the Airy Transit Circle.
The prime meridian at Greenwich is marked by a bronze sphere signed "Earth's Central Meridian" and attached to the top of the Greenwich Observatory's Earth rotation tripod.
[36] [37] It is also the reference meridian of the Global Positioning System operated by the U.S. Department of Defense , and of the European Galileo system.
[38] It is also the meridian used by the International Telecommunication Union for identifying locations on the Earth.
[39] It is not the meridian of the observer at the Airy Transit Circle; that is marked by the Airy Transit Telescope .
Instead, the surface of the Earth beneath the Airy Transit Circle meridian is rotated an additional half-degree, so that the stars appear in the same position each night.
This rotation is managed by the Airy Transit Equipment, which is managed by the UK Hydrographic Office .

[46] The second is the international standard for time imposed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), which is used in the ISO 8601 standard and by the Unix time system.
While ISO 8601 can be used in both scientific and commercial applications, the Unix time system, which represents time as the number of seconds that have elapsed since January 1, 1970 at 00:00:00 UTC, is more commonly used.
[47] It is not compatible with the ISO 8601 standard, which uses zoned hours, not the 24-hour clock , and the date and time formats yyyymmddhhmmss, not yyyymmdd-thh.
Both systems can coexist as the Unix time system is a special case of the ISO 8601 standard with a specific time zone offset.
The COBOL programming language uses an entirely different time format called TIME-OF-BASIC-TIME (TOBT), [48] which is widely used in business computing for financial applications, while the ISO 8601 standard is used in scientific computing .
Time in physics [ edit ] In physics, time is used as a coordinate in combination with the spatial coordinates to define a position in space.
[49] The theory of relativity tells us that time is relative and can be affected by gravity and speed.
Time is also used in the notation of quantum mechanics .
The Schrödinger equation is often used with time as a constant parameter, so that the evolution of a quantum system is described by a time-dependent wave function .
The wave function of a system is often abbreviated to a pure state vector.

 List of U.S. states by coastline - Wikipedia List of U.S. states by coastline From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Jump to: navigation , search It has been suggested that Coastal states be merged into this article.
( Discuss ) Proposed since November 2017.
States shaded dark blue have ocean coastline.
States shaded light blue have only Great Lakes coast States with no coastline are not included.
This is a list of U.S. states ranked by their coastline length.
States with no coastline are not included.
Two separate measurements are used: method 1 only includes states with ocean coastline and excludes tidal inlets; method 2 includes Great Lake coastline and the extra length from tidal inlets.
For example, method 2 counts the Great Bay as part of New Hampshire 's coastline, but method 1 does not.
The figures suffer from the inaccuracy inherent in all attempts at measuring coastlines but are nevertheless useful for comparison.
The data for method 1 were retrieved from a CRS Report for Congress [1] using data from U.S. Department of Commerce , National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration , The Coastline of the United States , 1975 .
This is based on measurements made using large-scale nautical charts .
The figure for Connecticut was arrived at separately and may not reflect the correct comparative distance.
These numbers exclude the Great Lakes coastlines.
The data for method 2 are from a list maintained by the Office of Ocean and Coastal Resource Management of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
The state coastline lengths were computed by an unspecified method that includes tidal areas not included in the first method.
[2] These numbers also include the Great Lakes coastlines, which do not have similar tidal areas.

 List of Prime Ministers of India - Wikipedia List of Prime Ministers of India From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Jump to: navigation , search Narendra Modi is the current (14th) Prime Minister of India , since 26 May 2014 The Prime Minister of India is the chief executive of the Government of India .
In India's parliamentary system , the Constitution names the President as head of state de jure , but his or her de facto executive powers are vested in the Prime Minister and his Council of Ministers .
Appointed and sworn-in by the President, the Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party or alliance that has a majority in the Lok Sabha , the lower house of India's Parliament .
[1] Since 1947, India has had fourteen Prime Ministers, fifteen including Gulzarilal Nanda who twice acted in the role.
The first was Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress party, [2] who was sworn-in on 15 August 1947, when India gained independence from the British .
Serving until his death in May 1964, Nehru remains India's longest-serving prime minister.
He was succeeded by fellow Congressman Lal Bahadur Shastri , whose 19-month term also ended in death.
Indira Gandhi , Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri in 1966 to become the country's first woman premier.
Eleven years later, she was voted out of power in favour of the Janata Party , whose leader Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress prime minister.
After he resigned in 1979, his former deputy Charan Singh briefly held office until Indira Gandhi was voted back six months later.
Indira Gandhi's second stint as Prime Minister ended five years later on the morning of 31 October 1984, when she was gunned down by her own bodyguards.
That evening, her son Rajiv Gandhi was sworn-in as India's youngest premier, and the third from his family .
Thus far, members of Nehru–Gandhi dynasty have been Prime Minister for a total of 37 years and 303 days.

The primary functions of the human skeleton are to provide support for the body, attach muscles to bones, protect our most vital organs from being damaged, and aid in the production of red blood cells .
The skeleton can be divided into the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton .
The axial skeleton is the part of the skeleton that is located on the body's front or back, and the appendicular skeleton is located on the body's outside.
The axial skeleton is made up of the vertebral column , the rib cage , the skull , and the sternum .
The appendicular skeleton is made up of the shoulder girdle , the pelvic girdle, the bones of the upper arm and thigh, and the bones of the forearm and leg.
The human skeleton performs six major functions; support, movement, protection, production of blood cells, storage of minerals, and endocrine regulation.
The human skeleton is not as sexually dimorphic as that of many other primate species, but subtle differences between sexes in the morphology of the skull , dentition , long bones , and pelvis exist.
In general, female skeletal elements tend to be smaller and less robust than corresponding male elements within a given population.
The human female pelvis is also different from that of males in order to facilitate childbirth .
Unlike most primates, human males do not have penile bones .

The Phenice method is commonly used to determine the sex of an unidentified human skeleton by anthropologists with 96% to 100% accuracy in some populations.

One of the most common is osteoporosis .
Also common is scoliosis , a side-to-side curve in the back or spine, often creating a pronounced "C" or "S" shape when viewed on an x-ray of the spine.
This condition is most apparent during adolescence, and is most common with females.
Arthritis [ edit ] Main article: Arthritis Arthritis is a disorder of the joints.
It involves inflammation of one or more joints.
When affected by arthritis, the joint or joints affected may be painful to move, may move in unusual directions or may be immobile completely.
The symptoms of arthritis will vary differently between types of arthritis.
The most common form of arthritis: Osteoarthritis can affect both the larger and smaller joints of the human skeleton.
The cartilage in the affected joints will degrade, soften and wear away.
This decreases the mobility of the joints and decreases the space between bones where cartilage should be.
Osteoporosis [ edit ] Main article: Osteoporosis Osteoporosis is a disease of bone where there is reduced bone mineral density , increasing the likelihood of fractures .
[11] Osteoporosis is defined by the World Health Organization in women as a bone mineral density 2.5 standard deviations below peak bone mass, relative to the age and sex-matched average, as measured by Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry , with the term "established osteoporosis" including the presence of a fragility fracture .
[12] Osteoporosis is most common in women after menopause , when it is called "postmenopausal osteoporosis", but may develop in men and premenopausal women in the presence of particular hormonal disorders and other chronic diseases or as a result of smoking and medications , specifically glucocorticoids .
[11] Osteoporosis usually has no symptoms until a fracture occurs.
[11] For this reason, DEXA scans are often done in people with one or more risk factors, who have developed osteoporosis and be at risk of fracture.
[11] Osteoporosis treatment includes advice to stop smoking, decrease alcohol consumption, exercise regularly, and have a healthy diet.
Calcium supplements may also be advised, as may Vitamin D .
When medication is used, it may include bisphosphonates , Strontium ranelate , and osteoporosis may be one factor considered when commencing Hormone replacement therapy .

* There are three types of cones that respond to different wavelengths of light (red, green, and blue)
* The arrangement of cones is not uniform and tends to concentrate in certain areas of the retina

When cerebrospinal fluid exits the cerebral aqueduct it flows through the **cisterna magna and subsequently into the central canal of the spinal cord** before reaching the subarachnoid space.

Additional Details:
* The cerebrospinal fluid flows from the lateral ventricles through the cerebral aqueduct (also called the septum pellucidum) to the third ventricle
* After entering the third ventricle, it passes through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle
* From the fourth ventricle, CSF flows into the central canal of the spinal cord
* The cisterna magna is a large fluid-filled space in the fourth ventricle that CSF flows into
* The central canal of the spinal cord serves as a pathway for CSF to flow from the fourth ventricle toward the lumbar cistern (lower part of the spinal cord)

In India's parliamentary system , the Constitution names the President as head of state de jure , but his or her de facto executive powers are vested in the Prime Minister and his Council of Ministers .
Appointed and sworn-in by the President, the Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party or alliance that has a majority in the Lok Sabha , the lower house of India's Parliament .
[1] Since 1947, India has had fourteen Prime Ministers, fifteen including Gulzarilal Nanda who twice acted in the role.
The first was Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress party, [2] who was sworn-in on 15 August 1947, when India gained independence from the British .
Serving until his death in May 1964, Nehru remains India's longest-serving prime minister.
He was succeeded by fellow Congressman Lal Bahadur Shastri , whose 19-month term also ended in death.
Indira Gandhi , Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri in 1966 to become the country's first woman premier.
Eleven years later, she was voted out of power in favour of the Janata Party , whose leader Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress prime minister.

Indira Gandhi's second stint as Prime Minister ended five years later on the morning of 31 October 1984, when she was gunned down by her own bodyguards.

[10] On August 27, 1963, the song was recorded over again at Pythian Records , this time with more orchestration and harmonies, and was released in October as a single by RCA in both the U.S. and the U.K. [11] [12] Where it was a moderate hit, peaking at number 48 on the Billboard Country Music chart , it was a big success in the U.K. where it peaked at number 3.
[13] On November 22, 1963, the song was recorded in London by John Barry and his orchestra.
[14] In 1964, Frank Sinatra included the song on his album It Might as Well Be Swing , accompanied by Count Basie .
[15] In 1965, Peggy Lee recorded the song for her album Love Letters , [16] and in 1967, Glen Campbell covered the song on his album Wichita Lineman .
[17] Tom Jones released a version in 1967, [18] as did Herman's Hermits on their album I'm Into Something Good .
[19] In 1968, the song was covered by the Chicks , [20] and are featured in the film The Longest Yard , starring Burt Reynolds .
[21] In 1976, a version was recorded by the French singer Roland Gerbeau .
[22] In 1977, a version was arranged and recorded by the Singers of West Virginia at the New Eden Church of Worship in Evanston, Illinois by Pastor Stan Jones [23] and was released as a single in Illinois .
[24] A live version of the song was performed by I See Stars on their 2006 album, The Light .
[25] A version was also recorded by the Canadian rocker Susan Aglukark for her 1998 album, "Under the Sparkling Sun".
[26] Alex Chilton recorded a version in 1967 that was released on his album Easy Going .
[27] A version was also released by the German band Bittere Liebe .
[28] In 2002, the American band Collective Soul recorded a version for their album, Clear .
[29] The British band Tinie Tempah featured a sample of the song in his 2012 single, " Electro ," which reached number one in the United Kingdom.
[30] [31] Arturo Tappin recorded a version in 2012 for his album, The Complete Studio Albums 1961–1989 .
[32] In 2013, the American band One Direction recorded a version of the song for their album, Up All Night .
[33] [34] Personal use and cover versions [ edit ] Over the years, many famous and not-so-famous artists have covered the song, including Bobby G, Johnny Kidd & the Pirates , Gerry & the Pacemakers , the Four Seasons , the Four Tops , Frank Sinatra , Brenda Lee , Billy Joel , Jennifer Holliday , Barry Manilow , Donny Osmond , Maureen McGovern , Perry Como , Nana Mouskouri , Celine Dion , John Paul Young , John Lennon , Nick Lawton, Rod Stewart , Van Morrison , Tommy Steele , Spanky and Our Gang , the Seeds , the Smugglers, the Holy Ground Crew, the Mutants, and Steppenwolf , among others.
[35] [36] The song's ubiquitous airplay on radio led Rudy Martin to write humorous lyrics called "The Song That Refuses to Die" in response, [37] which was recorded by Terry Bush in 1987 and reached number 89 on the Canadian "Easy Listening" chart.
[38] A strident, orchestral version was adopted by the Canadian television network CTV for its 1988 summer highlightreel, and became a hit single for singer-songwriter Jane Siberry in 1990.
[39] [40] In the same year, Leslie Jordan recorded a version as a single for use in the Canadian television series Working TV , and later included it on his 1991 album, Leslie Jordan Is Not Dead Yet .
[41] [42] In 1994, Nanci Griffith wrote and recorded a version of the song as a duet with Gary Morris for the soundtrack to the comedy film A League of their Own .
[43] [44] In 1995, Granger Smith included a version of the song on his album Windows Down .
[45] [46] In 2002, the American band The Cinematic Orchestra recorded a version for their album, Time's Ghost .
[47] [48] In 2007, the song was covered by the American band Ludo Lefebvre for his album Made in America .
[49] [50] In 2014, the British singer and songwriter Sam Smith included a version of the song on the soundtrack to the film Pride .
[51] [52] In the same year, the American band One Direction recorded a version of the song for their album, Up All Night .

When did australia get rid of the death penalty
Jump to: navigation , search Australia abolished the death penalty in 1973.
It was originally adopted in 1900, when Australia was a collection of British colonies .
The death penalty had been used occasionally in Australia between 1864 and 1900, usually for murder and in cases of piracy (there were several executions for piracy between 1693 and 1830).
However, it was not commonly used and was abolished in all jurisdictions in 1934, except for Western Australia, which did not abandon the death penalty until 1984.
Contents [ hide ] 1 History 1.1 Commonwealth 1.2 New South Wales 1.3 Victoria 1.4 Queensland 1.5 Western Australia 1.6 South Australia 1.7 Tasmania 1.8 Australian Capital Territory 1.9 Northern Territory 2 Public opinion 3 References 4 External links History [ edit ] Death sentences were carried out under Aboriginal customary law, although it is unknown how many people were executed.
The first executions carried out under European law in Australia took place in Western Australia in 1629, when Dutch authorities hanged the mutineers of the Batavia .
Capital punishment had been part of the legal system of Australia since British settlement and during the 19th century, crimes that could carry a death sentence included burglary, sheep stealing, forgery, sexual assaults, murder and manslaughter, and there is one reported case of someone being executed for "being illegally at large".
During the 19th century, these crimes saw about 80 people hanged each year throughout Australia.
Before and after federation, each state made its own criminal laws and punishments.
For a full list see: Main article: List of people legally executed in Australia Commonwealth [ edit ] In 1973 the Death Penalty Abolition Act 1973 [2] of the Commonwealth abolished the death penalty for federal offences.
It provided in Section 3 that the Act applied to any offence against a law of the Commonwealth, the Territories or under an Imperial Act, and in s.
4 that "[a] person is not liable to the punishment of death for any offence".
No executions were carried out under the bridge of the federal government and the passage of the Death Penalty Abolition Act 1973 [3] saw the death penalty replaced with life imprisonment as their maximum punishment.
Since the Commonwealth effects of utilising this Act no more individuals have been exposed to the death penalty and it is now replaced with life imprisonment.
On 11 March 2010 Federal Parliament passed laws that prevent the death penalty from being reintroduced by any state or territory in Australia.
[1] Neither the Commonwealth nor any of the states will extradite or deport a prisoner to another jurisdiction if they will face the death penalty.
A recent case involving this was the case of American Gabe Watson, who was convicted of the manslaughter of his wife in North Queensland, and faced capital murder charges in his home state of Alabama.
His deportation was delayed until the government received assurances that he would not be executed if found guilty.
New South Wales [ edit ] The last execution in New South Wales was carried out on 24 August 1939, when John Trevor Kelly was hanged at Sydney's Long Bay Correctional Centre for the murder of Marjorie Constance Sommarlad.
New South Wales abolished the death penalty for murder in 1955, but retained it as a potential penalty for treason , piracy , and arson in naval dockyards until 1985.
New South Wales was the last Australian State to formally abolish the death penalty for all crimes.
Victoria [ edit ] Old Melbourne Gaol gallows Victoria’s first executions occurred in 1842 when two Aboriginal men, Tunnerminnerwait and Maulboyheenner, were hanged outside the site of the Melbourne Gaol for the killing of two whalers in the Westernport district.
[5] Ronald Ryan was the last man executed at Pentridge Prison and in Australia.
Ryan was hanged on 3 February 1967 after being convicted of the shooting death of a prison officer during a prison escape from Pentridge Prison , Coburg, Victoria in 1965.
Ryan was the last of 186 executions.
[6] Victoria was also the state of t
After Victoria abolished capital punishment in 1975 the beam used to execute prisoners was removed from Old Melbourne Gaol and put into storage.
It was reinstalled at the Old Melbourne Gaol Museum in 2000.
[10] Queensland [ edit ] A total of 94 people were hanged in the Moreton Bay/Queensland region from 1830 until 1913.
[11] The last person hanged was Ernest Austin , for the rape and murder of an 11-year-old girl.
Only one woman was hanged, Ellen Thompson (1887).
She was convicted of murdering her husband with the help of her lover.
In 1922 Queensland became the first part of the British Commonwealth to abolish the death penalty.
[12] Western Australia [ edit ] In Western Australia , the first legal executions were under Dutch VOC law on 2 October 1629 on Long Island, Houtman Abrolhos (near Geraldton ), when Jeronimus Corneliszoon and six others were hanged as party to the murder of 125 men, women and children.
Following British colonization, between 1833 and 1855 executions by firing squad and hanging were performed at a variety of places, often at the site of the offence.
Even with the construction of the new Perth Gaol in 1855 as the main execution site in the state, executions were also carried out at various country locations until 1900.
In 1886 the Fremantle Prison was handed over to the colonial government as the colony's major prison; from 1889 43 men (and 1 woman, Martha Rendell ) were hanged there.
The first execution under British law was that of Midgegooroo , who on 22 May 1833 was executed by firing squad while bound to the door of the original Perth Gaol.
John Gavin , a Parkhurst apprentice , was the first British settler to be executed in Western Australia.
In 1844 he was hanged for murder at the Fremantle Round House , at the age of fifteen.
Bridget Larkin was the first woman to be executed in Western Australia, for the murder of John Hurford , in 1855.
The last execution was that of Eric Edgar Cooke on 26 October 1964 at Fremantle Prison .
Cooke had been convicted on one count of murder, but evidence and his confessions suggested he had committed many more.
The last sentence of death in Western Australia (indeed anywhere in Australia) was passed in 1984, [13] [14] [15] but the female killer ( Brenda Hodge ) [16] in question had her sentence commuted to imprisonment for life, as was customary by this stage.
Capital punishment was formally removed from the statutes of the state with the passage of the Acts Amendment (Abolition of Capital Punishment) Act 1984.
South Australia [ edit ] The Adelaide Gaol was the site of forty-four hangings, from Joseph Stagg on 18 November 1840 to Glen Sabre Valance , murderer and rapist, on 24 November 1964 and three executions also occurred at Mount Gambier Gaol .
Two Ngarrindjeri men were controversially executed by hanging along the Coorong on 22 August 1840, after a drumhead court-martial conducted by Police Commissioner O'Halloran on the orders of Governor George Gawler .
The men were found to be guilty of murdering the twenty-five survivors of the shipwreck Maria a few months before.
[17] Elizabeth Woolcock , the only woman ever to have been executed under South Australian law, was hanged on 30 December 1873.
Her body was not released to the family and was buried between the inner and outer walls of the prison, identified by a number and the date of the execution.
In 1976, the Criminal Law Consolidation Act was modified so that the death sentence was changed to life imprisonment.
Tasmania [ edit ] In the early days of colonial rule Tasmania, then known as Van Diemen's Land , was the site of penal transports.
Mary McLauchlan was convicted in 1830 for infanticide; she was sentenced to both death and dissection.
[18] [19] She was the first woman to be hanged in Tasmania.
The last execution was in 1946, that of serial murderer and rapist Frederick Thompson.
The death penalty was abolished in 1968.
[20] Australian Capital Territory [ edit ] No executions were carried out in the Australian Capital Territory, where federal legislation abolished capital punishment in 1973.
Northern Territory [ edit ] Aborigines who lived in the Northern Territory came under the European law of Australia [ citation needed ] even though they did not have any contact with the government [ citation needed ] .
There were several outcries over Aborigines receiving mandatory death sentences for murder [ citation needed ] , leading to the passage of the Crimes Ordinance 1934 [ citation needed ] which allowed for discretionary sentences when both the accused and the victim were Aboriginal.
The last execution was a double hanging in 1952, and the death penalty was abolished 1973.
[21] Public opinion [ edit ] In Australia capital punishment was banned on a state-by-state basis through the 20th century.
Despite the ban, polls have indicated varying support for the reintroduction of the practice.
A 2005 Bulletin poll showed that most Australians supported capital punishment.
The Australian National University 's 2007 Electoral Survey found that 44 per cent of people thought the death penalty should be reintroduced, while only 38 per cent disagreed.
In the recent case of the Bali bombers , then prime minister John Howard stated that Australians expected their execution by Indonesia.
[22] [23] On occasion the issue of capital punishment is published in the media or is subject to media and public support and scrutiny.
Most occasions where capital punishment is brought up in the media, it is regarding current cases of intense media coverage regarding murder, rape and in extreme circumstances such as terrorism.
On various occasions, the media and public express support for capital punishment for the most heinous of crimes including mass murder such as in the cases of the Milat Backpacker Murders and the Bryant Port Arthur massacre , in which a total of 42 people were killed stirring strong emotions as to whether or not to reintroduce the death penalty.
A similar surge in public support for reintroduction occurred when Lindy Chamberlain was convicted of murdering her baby Azaria in 1982, although it was subsequently shown that she was not guilty.
This miscarriage of justice has been used as a powerful example of the risks of the death penalty.
However, no person of significant stature or influence has advocated the death penalty for quite some time since the last execution in 1967.
The death penalty was completely abolished in Australia with the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Torture Prohibition and Death Penalty Abolition) Bill 2009 passing the Australian Senate without amendments in March 2010.
[24] In 2009 a public opinion survey was conducted by Roy Morgan Research where responders were given the question: "In your opinion, should the penalty for murder be death or imprisonment?" The surveyors conducted the poll for people from 14 and onwards in age with around 687 people completing the survey for publication.

1993 54 36 10 August 1995 53 36 11 November 2005 27 66 7 December 2005 25 69 6 August 2009 23 64 13 In 2014 another public opinion survey was conducted by Roy Morgan Research where responders were given the question: “If a person is convicted of a terrorist act in Australia which kills someone should the penalty be death?” The surveyors conducted the poll with a cross-section of 1,307 Australians.
The poll showed a small majority of Australians (52.5%) favoured the death penalty for deadly terrorist acts in Australia while 47.5% didn’t.
This was a significant increase from 2009 when only 23% of Australians supported the death penalty being imposed for convicted murderers.

The Stonewall riots occurred on June 28, 1969, when police raided the Stonewall Inn , a gay bar in New York City's Greenwich Village.
Though similar raids were commonplace at the time, the resistance showed a new determination among gay individuals and their allies, leading to the beginning of the modern gay rights movement .
[1] [2] The riots spilled onto the streets in the early hours of June 29, 1969, and continued for several days.
The event became a rallying cry for gay rights activists around the world and is now celebrated as the anniversary of Stonewall, known as Stonewall Day or Gay Pride Day .
Stonewall (the name is a misnomer) was a popular bar in its time, but the riot marked a turning point in gay American history.
[3] [4] [5] [6] Contents [ hide ] 1 Background 1.1 Homosexuality in 20th-century United States 1.2 Homophile activism 1.3 Before Stonewall 2 The Stonewall 2.1 Riots 2.2 Aftermath 2.3 Legacy 3 See also 4 References 5 Further reading 6 External links Background [ edit ] Homosexuality in 20th-century United States [ edit ] Further information: Gay America The history of homosexuals in the United States is a history of their marginalization .
[7] By the 1950s, gay men and lesbians were heavily represented in the social and economic spheres of major American cities.
Many celebrities were openly gay or gay icons for subcultures, particularly in the world of fashion, where gay designers and editors influenced trends.
Many were open about their homosexuality, including many famous actors, designers, and writers.
Several publications catered to the gay community, including notable newspapers such as the New York Eagle and the Los Angeles Herald-Express [gay press] and magazines such as Screw .
Others included The Ladder and The Gay Magazine .
[8] [9] Many gay bars and bookstores provided services that were otherwise unavailable to gays and lesbians, including bookstores like The Cabaret , and blues clubs like Monoxide .
[10] [11] Many gays and lesbians had come out to their families, and to friends who had previously been in the dark about the sexual orientation of the individuals in their lives.
A large percentage of gays and lesbians lived in committed, long-lasting relationships.
Many homosexuals had children.
The gay population was also growing among the young, as more and more teenagers experimented with sexuality.
[12] Homophile activism [ edit ] Activists participate in a 1970 demonstration for rights for gay Americans in New York's Central Park .
At the time of the Stonewall riots, there were already gay rights groups in several cities across the United States.
These groups were largely composed of heterosexual allies of gay people, rather than gay people themselves.
[13] Two organizations were founded specifically to promote homosexual rights at the time of the Stonewall riots: the Los Angeles GLF , formed in October 1969, and the New York City chapter of the Daughters of Bilitis , which had been founded in 1955.
However, it was the Stonewall riots that finally galvanized gay Americans to organize themselves on a national level.
[14] After the Stonewall riots, these and other groups quickly began to expand their activities.
The first nationwide organization specifically focused on gay rights in the United States was the National Gay Task Force (NGTF), formed in 1973.
[15] It was created by combining two previously all-volunteer, nationwide organizations: the Gay Activists Alliance (GAA) and the National Gay Liberation Front (NGLF).
[16] In 1974, at the request of the National Gay Task Force, the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) admitted gay members, and subsequently voted to expel all heterosexual members, effectively making it an all-gay organization.
[17] [18] The Stonewall, named for the Stonewall Inn, a popular gay bar in New York City, became a symbol of gay activism and is now celebrated as a gay icon .
[19] [20] Stonewall (the name is a misnomer) was a popular bar in its time, but the riot marked a turning point in gay American history.

[12] Homophile organizations existed by the 1950s, although they were relatively small and often had limited impact.
They were able to exert some influence on policy in certain cities and counties regarding municipalities with a large gay population, and they helped to improve the social acceptance of gays and lesbians in those areas.
[12] Their influence peaked in the late 1950s and 1960s, when they helped more than 100 gay men and lesbians into the lives of thousands of other gay men and lesbians in major cities across America.

 The following year, the event started to be broadcast on pay-per-view [1] and thus became one of WWE's "big four" pay-per-views, along with WrestleMania , Survivor Series , and SummerSlam .
The men's Royal Rumble match is usually located at the top of the card , though there have been exceptions, such as the 1988 , 1996 , 1997 , 1998 , 2006 , 2013 , and 2018 events.
[2] Due to the Rumble match taking up a large amount of time (most Rumble matches last roughly one hour), the Rumble event tends to have a smaller card than most other pay-per-view events, which routinely have six to eight matches per card.
The 2008 Royal Rumble was the first WWE pay-per-view to be available in high-definition .
[3] The 2018 Royal Rumble was the first to feature a women's Royal Rumble match, which was the main event for that year.
Match The Royal Rumble is based on the classic Battle Royal match, in which a number of wrestlers (traditionally 30) aim at eliminating their competitors by tossing them over the top rope, with both feet touching the floor.
[4] [5] WWE's version of the Battle Royal Royal Rumble differs from the traditional Royal Rumble in that Elimination Chamber wrestlers are not required to stay outside the ring until they are eliminated; instead, they can choose to stay in and fight other wrestlers to prolong their own time in the match.
[6] The winner of the event is the last wrestler remaining after all others have been eliminated.
[4] According to Hornswoggle , who worked for WWE from 2006 until 2016 and participated in two Rumbles, participants may learn their eliminations by knowing the two wrestlers who are eliminated before them and which wrestlers are entering the Royal Rumble in between their elimination.
[7] The Royal Rumble differs from the classical Battle Royal as the contestants do not enter the ring at the same time, but instead are assigned entry numbers, usually via a lottery , although desirable spots are occasionally assigned by other means, the most common being winning a match.
This lottery is usually staged right before the event begins.
[4] The match begins with the two wrestlers who have drawn entry numbers one and two, with the remaining wrestlers entering the ring at regular timed intervals, either 90 seconds or two minutes, according to their entry number.
[4] This format is credited to Pat Patterson .
[8] To date, only four men who have been one of the starting wrestlers have won the Royal Rumble: Shawn Michaels , Vince McMahon , Chris Benoit , and Rey Mysterio .
The most common number to win is number 27.
Royal Rumble match in 2010 The Royal Rumble match traditionally involves 30 wrestlers and usually lasts an hour, with the longest match, at the 2011 event , lasting over one hour and nine minutes of a three-hour pay-per-view.
[9] However, the first televised Rumble match , contested in 1988, involved only 20 men, [10] and lasted 33 minutes of the two-hour broadcast.
[9] The 1998 Royal Rumble nominally had the traditional 30-man field, but only 28 individual wrestlers competed; Mick Foley entered the Royal Rumble match three different times—first as Cactus Jack, then as Mankind, and finally as Dude Love.
[11] The 2011 Royal Rumble was the first and only to have a 40-man field, [12] out of whom Alberto Del Rio was victorious.
The 2018 Royal Rumble was the first to feature a women's Royal Rumble match, with Stephanie McMahon making the official announcement on the December 18, 2017 edition of Raw .
[13] The women's Royal Rumble match has all of the same rules as the men's match, including having 30 participants.
[14] [15] Steve Austin holds the current record for most Royal Rumble match wins, with three.
[16] The match has no stipulations or rules other than that elimination must occur by a participant being placed over the top rope and both feet touching the floor.
A wrestler who only touches the floor with one foot is not eliminated from the match, a rule which greatly affected the 1995 match, allowing Shawn Michaels to re-enter the ring and win the match.
This has been popularized by Kofi Kingston , who although has not won a match, he has found various ways to keep both of his feet from touching the floor.
[17] Subsequently, a wrestler who exits the ring without going over the top rope is not eliminated from the contest.
For example, during the 1999 match, both Vince McMahon and Steve Austin left the ring, only to return later in the match.
[18] In the 1994 match, the last two participants, Bret Hart and Lex Luger , were declared co-winners when it was decided that both of their feet touched the floor at exactly the same time.
[19] A similar situation occurred in the 2005 match.
However, the match was instead restarted after Batista and John Cena eliminated each other at the same time (as their simultaneous elimination was actually an accident); Batista eliminated Cena afterwards to win the match.
[20] Though various referees are charged with observing the match, some eliminations have gone unnoticed to allow the eliminated participants to sneak back into the ring to continue.
Steve Austin was able to win in this way during the 1997 match after re-entering following an unacknowledged elimination and eventually tossed Bret Hart , who was the last legal wrestler in the ring, over the top.
[21] Although the vast majority of eliminations are caused by active participants, eliminations caused by other means have occurred, and have been ruled legitimate, including self-eliminations (such as Andre the Giant jumping out of the ring after seeing a snake in 1989, Kane eliminating himself in 1999, and Drew Carey eliminating himself in 2001; however, Randy Savage 's jump over the top rope in 1992 was not ruled as self-elimination), elimination from previously-eliminated participants (such as The Undertaker eliminating Maven in 2002, Kurt Angle eliminating Shawn Michaels in 2005, Kane eliminating CM Punk in 2014, and The Wyatt Family eliminating Brock Lesnar in 2016), and elimination from non-participants (such as Shane McMahon eliminating Shawn Michaels in 2006 and The Miz eliminating John Cena in 2011).
Furthermore, if an injured wrestler is taken away by medical staff, he can return to the match as long as the match is still ongoing (such as Steve Austin in 1999 or Roman Reigns in 2016), but if the match ends without the injured wrestler returning, he is deemed eliminated (such as Scotty 2 Hotty in 2005 or Curtis Axel in 2015).
Prize Since 1993, the winner of the Royal Rumble match is traditionally awarded a title match for WWE's top championship at WrestleMania – presently, there are two top championships, the Universal Championship on Raw and the WWE Championship on SmackDown .
[22] Similarly, the winner of the women's Royal Rumble match (first contested in 2018) is awarded a match at WrestleMania for either of WWE's top two women's championships, the Raw Women's Championship or the SmackDown Women's Championship .
[13] With the brand extension introduced in mid-2002, the 30 male entrants from 2003 to 2006 consisted of 15 wrestlers from both the Raw and SmackDown brands.
At first, the winner of the match received a shot at their brand's top champion.
[23] Starting in 2004, the Rumble winner had the option of challenging any brand's champion.
For instance, Chris Benoit switched brands after winning the 2004 Royal Rumble and won the World Heavyweight Championship at WrestleMania XX .
[23] From 2007 to 2010, participants from the ECW brand competed along with the Raw and SmackDown brands, with the ECW World Championship added as an option for the winner to challenge for, although no winners ever did.
[24] During ECW's participation, the entries for each brand were not evenly divided.
[25] The ECW Championship was deactivated in 2010, and the World Heavyweight Championship was unified into the WWE Championship in 2013, leaving the latter as the only title to challenge for until July 2016, when the brand extension returned.
With the new brand extension, the winner of the 2017 event earned a match for their brand's top championship, Raw's Universal Championship or SmackDown's WWE Championship, but beginning in 2018, the winner has a choice.

Novak goes to Las Vegas and gambles away the money, but wins it back and then some.
He uses most of it to buy the Boston Red Sox, who own the rights to his betting tips, freeing them from their contract with his bookie.
Returning to Boston, Novak is greeted by Felicia and told by her that she is pregnant with their first child.
Novak returns the money to the bookie, who is the head of a Boston crime organization.
Novak is then invited to a party by the mayor of Boston, who makes Novak his campaign manager in an attempt to get Novak's friend, Ray McGuire ( Denis Leary ) to throw the election to prevent Novak from revealing a secret that could ruin McGuire's mayoral campaign.
Novak reveals the secret, and McGuire is elected mayor.
Novak then decides to return the money to the mayor, but is followed by a gunman who shoots him.
Novak is treated by a doctor ( Michael J.
Roth ) who tells him that he is unlikely to die, but his wife Ellen ( Elisabeth Shue ) fears the worst.
Novak's mother ( Mare Winningham ) arrives and argues with Felicia.
Novak wakes from a coma and listens to his mother apologize to Felicia.
Novak goes outside and says goodbyes to his mother, and then lights a cigarette.

[2] The soundtrack album was released on November 17, 2008, by Interscope Records and Star Sound Label Group in the United Kingdom and on November 19 in the United States.
The album contains instrumental and vocal tracks, and includes reworks of older Rahman songs such as " Tiruppati ", " Kena Kena ", " Sivagiri ", and "Oru Sanvilai".
It features songs sung by Sukhwinder Singh, Mahalaxmi Iyer, Vijay Prakash, Tanvi Shah, and Mahalaxmi.
The soundtrack received universally favorable reviews from critics, who cited it as one of the best soundtrack albums of all time.
R.
Rahman's work on the film and soundtrack was praised by critics, who remarked that the soundtrack "works as a complete unit".
[3] [4] It earned two Academy Awards for Best Original Song for "Jai Ho" and Best Original Score .
[5] "Jai Ho" also won the Grammy Award for Best Song Written for a Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media and the Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song .
The song's lyrics were inspired by the 2006 Pakistani crash of a plane , and the song won a Grammy Award for Best Song Written for a Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media .
[6] "Jai Ho" won the BAFTA Award for Best Music .
[7] The song features vocals from Singh, Iyer, Prakash, and Shah.
It includes elements of Indian music, such as the sitar and tabla , and Western music, such as an orchestra and rock music .
[8]-production of the song includes a mix of traditional Indian instruments and electronic instruments .
[9] [10] Indian singer Tanvi Shah wrote and provided vocals for a Spanish section of the song.
[11] According to Rahman, "Jai Ho was meant to be a hope song, a song to bring in positive energy.
It was meant to be a song that would get people on their feet and make them dance." [12] Rahman stated that he included the song in the film "because I wanted to do a song with my daughter.
She was very excited about it, and I was thinking of doing a song with her because she was growing up and wanted to get into the film industry".
[13] Rahman revealed that he sent the song to "a few people" before deciding to keep it for Slumdog Millionaire .
"He [Danny Boyle] didn't want to let go of the song and he told me, 'I want to use this song in the film'.
So I had to convince him that we couldn't do that because we didn't have the rights to the song yet, although we had a very good relation with the publishers of the song, which was A.
R.
Rahman and the publishers were very good friends".
[13] Boyle told Rahman that if he liked the song, he would give him the rights to use it in the film.
Rahman states that Boyle "does a great job" in directing him.
[12] Rahman noted that "There's a lot of pressure when you know the song is going to be sung by someone else.
I wanted to do it justice and I'm very happy that I did".
[13] He originally planned to use "Uijadha Uijadha" (உயர்த்தா உயர்த்தா) from Sachiin's 2004 song " Oru San Vilai ", which is also in Tamil.
Rahman modified the tune and created new lyrics.

This is a list of U.S. states ranked by their coastline length.
States with no coastline are not included.
Two separate measurements are used: method 1 only includes states with ocean coastline and excludes tidal inlets; method 2 includes Great Lake coastline and the extra length from tidal inlets.
For example, method 2 counts the Great Bay as part of New Hampshire 's coastline, but method 1 does not.
The figures suffer from the inaccuracy inherent in all attempts at measuring coastlines but are nevertheless useful for comparison.
The data for method 1 were retrieved from a CRS Report for Congress [1] using data from U.S. Department of Commerce , National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration , The Coastline of the United States , 1975 .
This is based on measurements made using large-scale nautical charts .
The figure for Connecticut was arrived at separately and may not reflect the correct comparative distance.
These numbers exclude the Great Lakes coastlines.
The data for method 2 are from a list maintained by the Office of Ocean and Coastal Resource Management of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
The state coastline lengths were computed by an unspecified method that includes tidal areas not included in the first method.
[2] These numbers also include the Great Lakes coastlines, which do not have similar tidal areas.

The song became a huge hit, reaching #6 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1974.

The Mystery Spot is between the Santa Cruz Mountains and the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk , popular tourist spots .

The illusion experienced by visitors results from the oddly tilted environment as well as standing on a tilted floor.
Inside the tilted room of the Mystery Spot, misperceptions of the height and orientation of objects occur.
[4] Even when people are standing outside on a level ground, the slant of the building in the background causes misperceptions as humans judge the height of people using the slant of the roof rather than the true horizon.
[5] These visual illusions include balls rolling uphill and people leaning farther than normally possible without falling down.
[6] Psychologists at Berkeley state that all of the misperceptions stem from the simple fact that the house is slanted at a 20 degree angle.
[7] Professor William Prinzmetal states, “When the perceiver's body also is tilted, the distorting impact on vision is greatly magnified- up to two or three times.” [8] Another point he makes is that distorted orientation causes other senses to fall back while your visual senses become heightened.
[9] People standing at impossible angles and water flowing uphill are related to the angle at which the house sits on.
Other suggestions have been proposed to explain the reason behind The Mystery Spot’s odd gravitational rules and illusions.
Tour guides suggest that “a meteor which fell in ancient days and left a magic circle” is the cause behind the mystery, [10] and suggest that an electromagnetic field on the hill deters wildlife .

(June 2011) ( Learn how and when to remove this template message ) Diagram showing the basic physiologic mechanisms of the kidney In renal physiology , ultrafiltration occurs at the barrier between the blood and the filtrate in the glomerular capsule ( Bowman's capsule ) in the kidneys .
As in nonbiological examples of ultrafiltration , pressure (in this case blood pressure ) and concentration gradients lead to a separation through a semipermeable membrane (provided by the podocytes ).
The Bowman's capsule contains a dense capillary network called the glomerulus .
Blood flows into these capillaries through the afferent arterioles and leaves through the efferent arterioles .
The high hydrostatic pressure forces small molecules in the tubular fluid such as water , glucose , amino acids , sodium chloride and urea through the filter, from the blood in the glomerular capsule across the basement membrane of the Bowman's capsule and into the renal tubules .
This process is called ultrafiltration; the resulting fluid, virtually free of large proteins and blood cells, is referred to as glomerular filtrate, or ultrafiltrate.
[1] Further modification of ultrafiltrate, by reabsorption and secretion , transforms it into urine .
Glomerular pressure is about 75 millimeters of mercury (10 kPa ).
It is opposed by osmotic pressure (30 mmHg, 4.0 kPa) and hydrostatic pressure (20 mmHg, 2.7 kPa) of solutes present in capsular space.
This difference in pressure is called effective pressure (25 mmHg, 3.3 kPa).
In hemodialysis centers, ultrafiltration takes place on the hemodialysis machines when the venous pressure is greater than the transmembrane pressure (TMP).
This cleans whole blood while keeping its blood cells intact.
Contents [ hide ] 1 Selectivity 2 Slow continuous ultrafiltration 3 See also 4 References Selectivity [ edit ] See also: Table of permselectivity for different substances The structures of the layers of the glomerulus determine their permeability -selectivity ( permselectivity ).
For instance, small ions such as sodium and potassium pass freely, while larger plasma proteins, such as hemoglobin tetramers, haptoglobin bound hemoglobin and albumin have practically no permeability at all.
Also, negatively charged molecules will pass through far less frequently than positively charged ones.
Slow continuous ultrafiltration [ edit ] Slow Continuous Ultrafiltration (SCUF) is an artificial method which approximately mimics the ultrafiltration function of the kidneys.
SCUF is a continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) generally used to remove fluid from fluid overloaded patients suffering acute renal failure .
During SCUF blood is removed from the body and is passed through an extracorporeal circuit through a hemofilter and a predetermined percentage of plasma water is removed based upon a prescription.
Typically, no more than 2 liters an hour of fluid is removed.
The remaining blood is returned to the patient.
Unlike hemodialysis , hemofiltration and hemodiafiltration , no dialysate or replacement fluids are used in SCUF.

 List of countries by oil production - Wikipedia List of countries by oil production From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Jump to: navigation , search This is a list of countries by oil production , as compiled from the U.S. Energy Information Administration database for calendar year 2016, tabulating all countries on a comparable best-estimate basis.
Compared with shorter-term data, the full-year figures are less prone to distortion from periodic maintenance shutdowns and other seasonal cycles.
The volumes in the table represent crude oil and lease condensate , the hydrocarbon liquids collected at or near the wellhead.
The volumes in the table do not include biofuel .
They also do not include the increase in liquid volumes during oil refining ("refinery gain"), or liquids separated from natural gas in gas processing plants ( natural gas liquids ).
[1] Under this definition, total world oil production in 2016 averaged 80,622,000 barrels per day.
Approximately 68% came from the top ten countries, and an overlapping 44% came from the fourteen current OPEC members, highlighted with blue shading in the table below.
For many years, the top three producers have been (alphabetically) Russia , Saudi Arabia , and the United States .
Each of these countries experienced major production declines at different times in the past, but since 2014 all three have been producing near their peak rates of 9 to 11 million barrels per day.

Compared with shorter-term data, the full-year figures are less prone to distortion from periodic maintenance shutdowns and other seasonal cycles.
The volumes in the table represent crude oil and lease condensate , the hydrocarbon liquids collected at or near the wellhead.
The volumes in the table do not include biofuel .
They also do not include the increase in liquid volumes during oil refining ("refinery gain"), or liquids separated from natural gas in gas processing plants ( natural gas liquids ).
[1] Under this definition, total world oil production in 2016 averaged 80,622,000 barrels per day.
Approximately 68% came from the top ten countries, and an overlapping 44% came from the fourteen current OPEC members, highlighted with blue shading in the table below.
For many years, the top three producers have been (alphabetically) Russia , Saudi Arabia , and the United States .
Each of these countries experienced major production declines at different times in the past, but since 2014 all three have been producing near their peak rates of 9 to 11 million barrels per day.
